t.7.69.1: Having heard the words of auspicious syllables spoken by me, O Rāma, that dweller of heaven, with palms joined in reverence, replied thus, O delight of the Raghus.
t.7.69.3: Long ago my father was the king of Vidarbha, a man of great glory and valour, renowned in the three worlds by the name of Sudeva.
t.7.69.2: Listen, O brahman, to this account of my joy and sorrow just as it happened, as you ask me, O twice-born; for it is indeed hard to overcome.
t.7.69.4: O Brahman, two sons were born to him by two wives: I am the one known as Śveta, and the younger was Suratha.
t.7.69.5: Then, when my father had gone to heaven, the citizens consecrated me as king; and there I ruled the kingdom righteously, with a well-composed mind.
t.7.69.6: Thus, O Brahman of excellent vows, thousands of years passed by for me as I ruled the kingdom and protected my subjects in accordance with dharma.
t.7.69.7: On a certain occasion I came to know the span of my life, O best of the twice-born; so, setting the law of time in my heart, I then went to the forest.
t.7.69.8: So I entered this impenetrable forest, devoid of beasts and birds, to practise austerities in the lovely vicinity of the lake.
t.7.69.9: Having consecrated my brother Suratha, lord of men, in the kingship, and having come to this lake, I practised austerities for a long time.
t.7.69.10: Having practised for three thousand years an austerity most difficult to perform, O great sage, I attained the unsurpassed world of Brahmā.
t.7.69.11: Then, O best of the twice-born, O most noble one, even while I dwelt in heaven, hunger and thirst tormented me, and so my senses were in anguish.
t.7.69.12: Having gone to the Grandfather, the foremost of the three worlds, he said: "O Blessed One, this world of Brahmā is free from hunger and thirst."
t.7.69.13: Of what deed is this the result, that I am overpowered by hunger and thirst? And what is to be my food, O god? Tell me that, O Grandsire.
t.7.69.14: But the Grandfather said to me: "O son of Sudeva, your food shall be your own savoury flesh; eat it always."
t.7.69.15: While you performed supreme austerity, you nourished only your own body. What is not sown never grows, O Śveta, O wise one.
t.7.69.16: Not even the smallest gift was given by you in the forest frequented by living creatures; therefore, dear child, though you have gone to heaven, you are tormented by hunger and thirst.
t.7.69.18: But when, O Śveta, the great sage Agastya, the invincible one, comes to that forest, then you shall be released from your distress.
t.7.69.17: So you must eat your own peerless body, well nourished by foods, as a nectar-sweet savor; that shall be your satisfaction.
t.7.69.19: For he, O gentle one, is able to deliver even the hosts of the gods; how much more, then, you, O mighty-armed one, who have fallen under the sway of hunger and thirst!
t.7.69.20: Having heard the decree of the blessed God of gods, I make my own body my loathsome food, O best of the twice-born.
t.7.69.21: O Brahman, though this has been eaten by me for many multitudes of years, it does not come to an end, O Brahmarṣi, and my satisfaction too is supreme.
t.7.69.22: Release me, who have fallen into misery, from this misery; for in this matter there is no refuge in any others except the twice-born Kumbhayoni.
t.7.69.23: O gentle one, best of the twice-born, accept this ornament for the sake of my deliverance; O brahmarṣi, please grant me this favour.
t.7.69.25: But when I had accepted that auspicious ornament, the former human body of the royal sage vanished.
t.7.69.24: Having heard the sorrowful words of that dweller in heaven, I accepted that excellent ornament for the sake of his deliverance.
t.7.69.26: But when that body had perished, the royal sage, the king, satisfied and rejoicing with supreme delight, went once more to heaven.
t.7.69.27: On that account, O Kākutstha, this divine ornament of wondrous appearance was given to me by him, who was equal to Śakra.
